title: Stream of Characters
description:
# Stream of Characters

Design a data structure that receives a stream of lowercase characters one at a time. After each new character, it must answer whether **any suffix** of the complete stream is equal to one of the given dictionary words.

For example, if `words = ["abc", "xyz"]` and the stream receives `a`, `x`, `y`, `z`, then the final query returns `true` because the current stream `axyz` has suffix `xyz`.

Implement the `StreamChecker` class:

* `StreamChecker(String[] words)` initializes the structure with the dictionary words.
* `boolean query(char letter)` appends `letter` to the stream and returns whether a dictionary word is now a suffix of the stream.

The stream is never reset between queries. A word can match even if it is shorter than another matching suffix, and duplicate words should not change the answers.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:** ["StreamChecker", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query", "query"]
[[["cd", "f", "kl"]], ["a"], ["b"], ["c"], ["d"], ["e"], ["f"], ["g"], ["h"], ["i"], ["j"], ["k"], ["l"]]
**Output:** [null, false, false, false, true, false, true, false, false, false, false, false, true]

## Constraints:

* `1 <= words.length <= 2000`
* `1 <= words[i].length <= 200`
* `words[i]` consists of lowercase English letters.
* `letter` is a lowercase English letter.
* At most `40000` calls will be made to `query`.

examples.output: [null, false, false, false, true, false, true, false, false, false, false, false, true]

solutions.name: Reverse Trie with Bounded Suffix Buffer
solutions.description:
## Approach
Insert every dictionary word into a trie in reverse order. Keep only the last `maxWordLength` streamed characters. For each query, walk the trie from the newest character backward; reaching a terminal node means some dictionary word is a suffix of the stream.

## Key Insight
A suffix of the stream read from right to left is a prefix in the reversed-word trie. Trimming the buffer to the longest dictionary word is safe because longer history can never be part of a future match.

## Complexity Analysis
Building the trie costs O(S), where S is the total length of all words. Each query walks at most L characters, where L is the longest word length, so Q queries cost O(Q * L). The trie stores O(S) nodes and the buffer stores O(L) characters.

solutions.name: Aho-Corasick Automaton
solutions.description:
## Approach
Build an Aho-Corasick automaton from the dictionary in normal order. Failure links point to the longest proper suffix state that is also a trie prefix. A query advances the current automaton state by one character and returns whether the current state or one of its failure ancestors is terminal.

## Key Insight
The automaton maintains every dictionary prefix that is also a suffix of the stream inside one state pointer. Propagating terminal flags along failure links turns suffix detection into a constant-time state check after each character.

## Complexity Analysis
Trie construction and failure-link BFS cost O(S). Once missing transitions are filled, each query performs one array transition and one output check, so Q queries cost O(Q). The automaton arrays use O(S) space.

solutions.name: Forward Trie Active States
solutions.description:
## Approach
Insert dictionary words in normal order. After each query character, start a new match from the root and also advance every currently active trie node. The active nodes represent dictionary prefixes that match suffixes ending at the current stream position.

## Key Insight
Instead of reading the stream backward, this route keeps all forward prefix matches alive. A terminal active node means the suffix ending at the newest character is exactly one dictionary word.

## Complexity Analysis
Building the trie costs O(S). Each query advances A active states, where A is the number of live prefix matches, so the query cost is O(A). The trie stores O(S) nodes and the active set stores O(A) nodes.

solutions.name: Length-Bucket Exact Suffix Sets
solutions.description:
## Approach
Group dictionary words by length in hash sets and keep a bounded stream buffer. After each query, test only the distinct dictionary lengths that fit inside the buffer, extracting the corresponding suffix and checking it in the set for that length.

## Key Insight
The prompt asks whether any dictionary word equals a suffix, so lengths are a useful first filter. This solution is deliberately simple and exact: it never relies on probabilistic hashing or trie traversal.

## Complexity Analysis
Building the length buckets costs O(S). Each query checks D distinct word lengths and may copy up to L characters per suffix, so the worst-case query cost is O(D * L). The dictionary buckets store O(S) characters and the stream buffer stores O(L).

solutions.name: Rolling Hash Buckets with Exact Verification
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store dictionary words by length and by a rolling hash of the reversed word. Keep the last `maxLength` stream characters. For each query, scan the buffer backward, updating the reversed suffix hash one character at a time. When a hash bucket matches the current suffix length, verify the candidate words exactly against the buffer.

## Key Insight
Scanning backward computes the same orientation as reversed dictionary words, so every suffix length can be checked during one pass over the recent stream. Exact verification after a hash match keeps the method deterministic even if two strings collide under 64-bit overflow arithmetic.

## Complexity Analysis
Preprocessing costs O(S). Each query scans at most L recent characters; exact verification adds C total candidate-character comparisons only when a hash bucket matches. The hash buckets store O(S) data and the buffer stores O(L).
